$comment: The lazy-streaming contract, shared by all five ports. Every language's test
suite LOADS this file — TypeScript src/LazyStream.spec.ts, Python
python/tests/test_lazy_contract.py, Rust rust/file/tests/lazy_contract_tests.rs,
Go go/file/lazy_contract_test.go, .NET dotnet/tests/SmooAI.File.Tests/LazyContractTests.cs.
Hand-mirrored literals are what let these five drift apart in the first place,
so do not copy these numbers into a test file: read them from here.
Not asserted here: how many bytes each port pulls off the *underlying source*
at construction. Every runtime reads ahead by a different amount (Node's
Readable highWaterMark, Go's bufio, .NET's Stream buffering), so that number is
not a portable contract — headBytes below is the buffer each port fills for
detection, and it is asserted directly against each port's exported constant.

fill.$comment: Source content is this ASCII pattern repeated, then truncated to sourceBytes.

cases.name: empty
cases.$comment: A zero-byte source. Empty S3 objects and zero-length uploads are real, and this is the boundary where "shorter than the head" degenerates — every port must still report an exact size of 0 rather than an unknown one.

cases.name: shorter-than-head
cases.$comment: Source ends inside the detection head, so the lazy constructor already holds the whole payload and behaves eagerly.

cases.name: exactly-head
cases.$comment: The head buffer fills exactly, so no port can tell EOF from a pending tail. All five stay lazy, with an empty tail.

cases.name: longer-than-head
cases.$comment: The ordinary lazy case: head pulled for detection, tail left in the source until bytes are demanded.

$comment: from_stream / createFromStream / NewFromStream / CreateFromStreamAsync buffer the
whole payload at construction, so size is exact and the bytes can be read more
than once. This is what separates them from the lazy constructor.
read()/readFileBytes() drains the tail and CACHES it, so a second call returns
the same bytes. iter_bytes()/iterBytes() drains the tail and does NOT cache — it
is the bounded-memory path, so the tail is gone once it has been iterated.
KNOWN DIVERGENCE, deliberately not papered over: the ports disagree on HOW they
report a read after a full iteration. Go returns an error ('no data available');
TypeScript, Python, Rust and .NET return an empty buffer. What all five agree on
— and what this fixture pins — is that the payload is never silently replayed,
which is the property that would corrupt data if it broke. Unifying the two
shapes changes a published API in four ports, so it is tracked separately
(pearl: unify post-iteration read across ports) rather than done here.
